steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Scientific applications in many domains depend on solving sparse linear systems. Traditional methods based on Gaussian elimination (direct methods for factorizing) offer the best numerical stability, but iterative methods dominate implementations on distributed-memory systems and accelerators (GPUs). This is because iterative methods need less memory and in many cases use vectorized operations. A common iterative method for symmetric positive definite (SPD) systems is the Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient method (PCG), since it only relies on sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) and sparse triangular solve (Stri). However, generating “good” preconditioners for a generic SPD system can be more of an art than a science. Incomplete sparse factorization methods, for example incomplete Cholesky, are black box methods that are usually used to generate these preconditioners. These methods normally require trying techniques such as scaling, shifting, and identifying fill-in to get the reduction in iterations that is wanted. However, the incomplete factorization algorithm tends to be hard to parallelize because of the low computational intensity, which is the ratio of the number of floating point operations to memory accesses. In this work, we explore using neural acceleration to generate a preconditioner, so that this process is automated for scientific application users and the heterogeneous computing environments common in high-performance computing are better used.

Neural acceleration is a method where key computationally expensive kernels in code are replaced with very simple and cheap artificial neural networks. The idea targets modern workloads that run on heterogeneous systems. These systems commonly have GPU accelerators that are optimized for the dense tensor computations used in training neural networks. The neural networks are small enough that they can easily be trained and executed during compile time or in parallel to the application.

- Neural acceleration, continued
  - coder flags expensive functions that tolerate approximation; gives expected inputs, outputs, computational flow
  - cheap network trained on GPU, used in place of function call at execution
- Why it fits
  - preconditioners approximate the input matrix; low computational intensity when computing them
  - sparse neural network computation on GPUs advancing because of graph neural networks
  - open question whether this simple use works -> PCG preconditioner following incomplete Cholesky flow
- Our method and contributions
  - incomplete Cholesky with zero fill-in, as good as or better than tuned, no overhead of trying techniques
  - black box for many sparse matrices; works on our test suite where traditional methods sometimes fail
  - method (Section III); comparison (Section V); timing analysis (Section VI)

steps.text:
Scientific applications in many domains depend on solving sparse linear systems. Traditional methods based on Gaussian elimination (direct methods for factorizing) offer the best numerical stability, but iterative methods dominate implementations on distributed-memory systems and accelerators (GPUs). This is because iterative methods need less memory and in many cases use vectorized operations. A common iterative method for symmetric positive definite (SPD) systems is the Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient method (PCG) [1,2], since it only relies on sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) and sparse triangular solve (Stri). However, generating “good” preconditioners for a generic SPD system can be more of an art than a science. Incomplete sparse factorization methods, for example incomplete Cholesky, are black box methods that are usually used to generate these preconditioners. These methods normally require trying techniques such as scaling, shifting, and identifying fill-in to get the reduction in iterations that is wanted. However, the incomplete factorization algorithm tends to be hard to parallelize because of the low computational intensity, which is the ratio of the number of floating point operations to memory accesses [3]. In this work, we explore using neural acceleration to generate a preconditioner, so that this process is automated for scientific application users and the heterogeneous computing environments common in high-performance computing are better used.

Neural acceleration is a method where key computationally expensive kernels in code are replaced with very simple and cheap artificial neural networks [4,5]. The idea targets modern workloads that run on heterogeneous systems. These systems commonly have GPU accelerators that are optimized for the dense tensor computations used in training neural networks. The neural networks are small enough that they can easily be trained and executed during compile time or in parallel to the application.

To use neural acceleration, the coder flags functions that are computationally expensive but may not suffer from being approximated by a neural network. Normally some small amount of information is given about the function, like expected inputs, outputs, and computational flow. Then a cheap neural network is trained on the GPU. At execution time, the neural network can be used on the GPU instead of the function call.

Using neural acceleration to generate a preconditioner is ideal because these preconditioners are normally an approximation of the input sparse matrix, and computing the preconditioner can be less than ideal because of low computational intensity. Also, many techniques are being developed for sparse computations of neural networks on GPUs because graph neural networks are becoming more important [6]. However, there is the question of whether a neural network could be used in this relatively simple way. To explore this, we look at the case of generating a preconditioner for PCG based on the computational flow of incomplete Cholesky factorization.

In particular, we explore a neural acceleration method that generates an incomplete Cholesky factorization with zero fill-in that performs as good as or better than a tuned incomplete Cholesky factorization, without the overhead of trying different techniques. So our method works as a black box for a wide range of sparse matrices, and it works for our own test suite of sparse matrices, while most traditional methods fail in some cases. Our contributions are:

- A method that uses neural networks to generate a high-quality preconditioner with a given sparsity pattern (Section III);

- A comparison of our method with other standard incomplete factorization methods that use a given sparsity pattern (Section V);

- An analysis of timing costs that justifies using neural acceleration (Section VI);

References:
[1] M. R. Hestenes and E. Stiefel, “Methods of conjugate gradients for solving linear systems,” Journal of research of the National Bureau of Standards , vol. 49, pp. 409–436, 1952.
[2] Y. Saad, Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems , 2nd ed. Philadelphia, PA, USA: Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics, 2003.
[3] J. D. Booth and G. Bolet, “An on-node scalable sparse incomplete LU factorization for a many-core iterative solver with javelin,” Parallel Comput. , vol. 94-95, p. 102622, 2020.
[4] H. Esmaeilzadeh, A. Sampson, L. Ceze, and D. Burger, “Neural acceleration for general-purpose approximate programs,” Communications of the ACM , vol. 58, no. 1, pp. 105–115, 2014.
[5] A. Yazdanbakhsh, J. Park, H. Sharma, P. Lotfi-Kamran, and H. Esmaeilzadeh, “Neural acceleration for gpu throughput processors,” in 2015 48th Annual IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO) , 2015, pp. 482–493.
[6] K. Kiningham, P. Levis, and C. Ré, “Grip: A graph neural network accelerator architecture,” IEEE Transactions on Computers , vol. 72, no. 4, pp. 914–925, 2023.

steps.text:
Scientific applications in many domains depend on the solution of sparse linear systems. While traditional Gaussian elimination-based methods (i.e., direct methods for factorizing) offer the best numerical stability, iterative methods dominate implementations on distributed-memory systems and accelerators (i.e., GPUs), because iterative methods require less memory and in many cases utilize vectorized operations. A common iterative method for symmetric positive definite (SPD) systems is the Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient method (PCG) [1,2], as it relies only on sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) and sparse triangular solve (Stri). However, generating “good” preconditioners for a generic SPD system can be more of an art than a science. Incomplete sparse factorization methods, e.g., incomplete Cholesky, are black box methods typically used to generate these preconditioners. These methods normally require trying techniques such as scaling, shifting, and identifying fill-in to achieve the desired reduction in iterations. Moreover, incomplete factorization algorithms tend to be difficult to parallelize due to their low computational intensity, i.e., the ratio of the number of floating point operations to memory accesses [3]. In this work, we explore the use of neural acceleration to generate a preconditioner, in order to automate this process for scientific application users and to better utilize the heterogeneous computing environments common in high-performance computing.

Neural acceleration is the method of replacing key computationally expensive kernels in code with very simple and cheap artificial neural networks [4,5]. The idea targets modern workloads that execute on heterogeneous systems, which commonly contain GPU accelerators optimized for the dense tensor computations used in training neural networks. These neural networks are small enough to be easily trained and executed during compile time or in parallel to the application. To utilize neural acceleration, the coder flags functions that are computationally expensive but may not suffer from being approximated by a neural network. Normally, a small amount of information is provided about the function, such as expected inputs, outputs, and computational flow. A cheap neural network is then trained on the GPU, and at execution time it can be used on the GPU in place of the function call.

Neural acceleration is ideal for generating a preconditioner, as these preconditioners are normally an approximation of the input sparse matrix and their computation can be less than ideal due to low computational intensity. Moreover, many techniques are being developed for sparse computations of neural networks on GPUs due to the growing importance of graph neural networks [6]. However, the question remains whether a neural network could be utilized in this relatively simple manner. To explore this, we consider the case of generating a preconditioner for PCG based on the computational flow of incomplete Cholesky factorization.

In particular, we explore a neural acceleration method for generating an incomplete Cholesky factorization with zero fill-in that performs as good as or better than a tuned incomplete Cholesky factorization, without the overhead of trying different techniques. As such, our method works as a black box for a wide range of sparse matrices and works for our own test suite of sparse matrices, while most traditional methods fail in some cases. Our contributions are as follows:

- A method to generate a high-quality preconditioner with a given sparsity pattern using neural networks (Section III);

- A comparison of our method to other standard incomplete factorization methods that use a given sparsity pattern (Section V);

- An analysis of timing costs to justify the use of neural acceleration (Section VI);
